title: Larry's Agent

jokes.text: Larry awkwardly pivots from movies to hobbies after the director refuses to discuss his film
jokes.setup: Larry introduces the topic of movies; the director deflects saying he didn't want to discuss it
jokes.punchline: Larry's graceless retreat: 'Uh, so, hobbies. You got some hobbies? What do you-- You have a hobby?'
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders cringe: he's the professional host who can't read the room. The pivot to 'hobbies' is perfectly inelegant — the frantic doubling of 'What do you-- You have a hobby?' captures his on-camera panic. Strong character integration because Larry's insecurity is the engine of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What is it, one of those heaven can wait type of movies?

jokes.text: The director says 'No' to having hobbies; audience laughs at the dead end Larry has walked himself into
jokes.setup: Larry desperately pivots to asking about hobbies as a safe topic
jokes.punchline: The director flatly says 'No' — he has no hobbies either
jokes.explanation: The single-word 'No' is a perfect economy laugh. The laugh track confirms this lands. Every escape route Larry tries gets blocked, escalating his humiliation. The deadpan delivery is the whole joke.

dialogue.line: No. No.

jokes.text: Larry uses the backdoor logic of 'movie merchandising' to get the director to reveal his film is 'a story about a man who's finding himself'
jokes.setup: Larry, blocked from discussing the movie directly, proposes working backwards from imaginary merchandise ('a so-and-so doll') to figure out what the film is
jokes.punchline: The director falls for it and says 'It's a story about a man who's finding himself' — the vaguest, most Hollywood-pretentious possible description
jokes.explanation: This is smart, layered comedy. Larry's merchandise gambit is itself funny — a genuinely lateral thinking interview trick that pays off beautifully. The punchline ('a man who's finding himself') is doubly funny: it's the most self-serious Hollywood-speak imaginable, AND the audience gets it as a laugh at Barry Levinson's expense without Larry having to be mean. Rewatch bonus because on re-view you appreciate how cleverly Larry maneuvers it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe if we knew that, we could figure out, Ah, it's a so-and-so doll. We'll work backwards.

jokes.text: Levinson finally reveals the film is 'a story about a man who's finding himself' — drawing laughter from the audience
jokes.setup: After elaborate negotiation about what CAN be said, Levinson finally gives a description — which turns out to be the most generic, non-committal Hollywood pitch cliché imaginable
jokes.punchline: 'It's a story about a man who's finding himself' — the audience laughs because this tells us nothing, and Levinson apparently couldn't even avoid being this bland after all the fuss
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff to the entire cold open bit, and it earns it. The comedy is layered: all that protective evasion, and what Levinson was guarding was a description so generic it could apply to any movie. Economy score is high because the punchline is perfectly brief. The audience laugh noted in the script is the show confirming the beat lands.

dialogue.line: It's a story about a man who's finding himself.

jokes.text: Larry immediately backstage tells Artie he handled the Levinson interview poorly; Artie says 'You always do this when you're renegotiating your contract'
jokes.setup: Larry is beating himself up about the interview
jokes.punchline: Artie cuts through the self-flagellation with a cynical, perfectly calibrated diagnosis: it's not about the interview — it's contract anxiety
jokes.explanation: Artie's function as the show's truth-teller is perfectly deployed here. The joke works on two levels: it's funny as a deflation of Larry's self-pity, AND it efficiently plants the episode's A-plot (contract negotiations). Rip Torn can deliver this with absolute authority. High character integration — only Artie can play Larry's therapist-manager-conscience this way.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Aw, bullshit. It was an excellent show.

jokes.text: Stevie Grant arrives and tells Larry 'you've got the network by the balls. They can't do this job.'
jokes.setup: Stevie is a slick young agent who shows up apparently just to schmooze
jokes.punchline: His pep talk is transparently hollow: 'They can't do this job' — flattering Larry with the most obvious agent-speak
jokes.explanation: Solid industry satire — the agent who shows up uninvited to drop sycophantic reassurances. Not exceptional, but it efficiently establishes Stevie as a type: the aggressive young Hollywood operator who's all flattery and no substance.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, you always do this when you're renegotiating your contract.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Fucking little snot. He's too busy playing with his balls to shake my hand. You're always supposed to shake a man's hand.'
jokes.setup: Stevie leaves without shaking Artie's hand, too busy working the room
jokes.punchline: Artie reduces all of Stevie's transgression to a single old-school grievance: the failure to shake hands — and delivers it with pure Artie moral authority
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Artie comedy. Rip Torn distills everything wrong with Stevie into one primal old-man code violation. The 'playing with his balls' line is a double-meaning accident that makes it even funnier. 'You're always supposed to shake a man's hand' is delivered with absolute conviction — as though it's the Sixth Commandment. High character integration: only Artie frames modern Hollywood moral corruption through handshake etiquette.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Just remember, you've got the network by the balls. They can't do this job.

jokes.text: After the warm Levinson reunion, Larry and Barry discuss who the guests are tomorrow night — Larry refuses to say
jokes.setup: Larry tells Barry that backstage he could freely share things he couldn't on-air — like tomorrow night's guests. 'Ask me who the guests are tomorrow night. I'd tell you.'
jokes.punchline: When Barry asks, Larry says 'I'd rather not say.' — mirroring the exact dynamic of the on-air interview
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most structurally elegant joke. Larry sets up a mirror of the Levinson interview — trying to prove that 'back here' is different — and then instantly recreates the same dynamic with himself in the director's role. The callback is perfectly constructed: it's not just a reference, it flips the power dynamic entirely. Larry becomes the one who won't say. Genuinely well-written comedy architecture that earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fucking little snot. He's too busy playing with his balls to shake my hand.

jokes.text: Artie challenges Hank's request to use the stage: 'Not shooting one of those fucking infomercials, are you?'
jokes.setup: Hank approaches Artie with a request to use the stage for a few weeks
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate suspicion: infomercial
jokes.explanation: Artie's cynicism about Hank's motives is always funny. The escalating guesses (infomercial, telethon) perfectly characterize how low Artie expects Hank's aspirations to be. 'The road' as a final revelation is itself funny — the road for what?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're always supposed to shake a man's hand.

jokes.text: Artie's escalating guesses: 'For one of those infomercials.' / 'Telethon?'
jokes.setup: Hank denies infomercial; Artie keeps guessing
jokes.punchline: Each guess ('infomercial,' 'telethon') is worse than Hank's actual plan — the comedy is in Artie's rock-bottom expectations for Hank
jokes.explanation: The escalation works because each guess implies Artie thinks Hank is one step lower on the showbiz ladder than reality. Efficient character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ask me who the guests are tomorrow night. I'd tell you.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Some songs, a few jokes, a little soft shoe, you know like Sammy used to do — but with a twist.' Artie: 'What's the twist?' Hank: 'I'm doing it.'
jokes.setup: Hank describes an elaborate Sammy Davis Jr.-style act and says there's a twist
jokes.punchline: The 'twist' is simply that Hank is the one performing it — as though Hank himself is the wild card that transforms the act
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is airtight — Hank builds anticipation for 'the twist' that will distinguish this from a standard lounge act — and the punchline is Hank's delusional self-regard perfectly crystallized. 'I'm doing it' lands because Hank believes his own involvement IS the twist. Artie's follow-up ('That's quite a twist, Hank') seals it with perfect deadpan. High quotability, perfect economy, maximum character integration. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Who are the guests tomorrow night?

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: I'd rather not say.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ok.

jokes.text: Artie: 'That's quite a twist, Hank.'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers 'I'm doing it' as though it's a revelation
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'That's quite a twist, Hank' — pure withering understatement
jokes.explanation: Artie's deadpan reaction is the comedic exclamation mark on Hank's punchline. The line itself is pure craft — four words that say everything. Rip Torn's delivery would be perfectly flat and contemptuous. Strong rewatch value because you hear a new layer of contempt each time.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Not shooting one of those fucking infomercials, are you?

jokes.text: Hank explains he can't rehearse at home because 'my place has that wall-to-wall shag'
jokes.setup: Artie asks why Hank can't rehearse at home
jokes.punchline: Hank's apartment has wall-to-wall shag carpet — a perfect, specific, dated detail that tells us everything about how Hank lives
jokes.explanation: The shag carpet detail is wonderful character comedy — deeply specific, slightly sad, perfectly Hank. It's the kind of lived-in world-building that elevates sitcom writing above formula.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: For one of those infomercials.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Telethon?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, to go on the road.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I'm sure your driveway will do just fine.'
jokes.setup: Hank pleads for stage access due to his shag carpet problem
jokes.punchline: Artie dismisses the entire enterprise with the most perfunctory possible solution: just use the driveway
jokes.explanation: Good Artie line — his contempt for the whole enterprise expressed through completely unhelpful advice. Economy is the strength here.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: A little soft shoe, you know like Sammy used to do, but with a twist. What's the twist? I'm doing it.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You've sunk all your money in that silly restaurant, and now you're completely fucked. 100% fucked.'
jokes.setup: Hank insists his act is a 'dream' and Artie should not 'demean' it
jokes.punchline: Artie ignores the emotional appeal entirely and delivers a clinical financial diagnosis with absolute certainty: '100% fucked'
jokes.explanation: The '100% fucked' kicker is perfect escalation — 'completely fucked' would have been fine, but Artie specifying the percentage transforms it into something more clinical and devastating. The dismissal of Hank's 'dream' framing in favor of blunt economic reality is pure Artie. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's quite a twist, Hank.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Artie, please.' / Artie: 'Aw, shit. All right, Hank.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just told Hank he's '100% fucked' and should use the driveway
jokes.punchline: Despite all his contempt, Artie folds immediately — a single 'please' from Hank is enough
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Artie, for all his gruffness, has a soft spot for Hank is a nice character beat. The 'Aw, shit' surrender is the comedic payoff — his bark is always worse than his bite where Hank is concerned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You need a hard surface, and my place has that wall-to-wall shag.

jokes.text: Hank invites Artie and Elaine to 'front row center at the El Toro Civic Arena exactly 4 weeks from tonight'
jokes.setup: Artie just granted Hank the stage grudgingly
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately upgrades from humble request to triumphant performer, presenting Artie with front-row seats to his imaginary arena show
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'El Toro Civic Arena' is doing heavy lifting — it's the most LA-adjacent, mid-tier venue imaginable. The gap between Hank's delusion (arena show in 4 weeks) and his actual situation (just begged to rehearse in the studio) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm sure your driveway will do just fine.

jokes.text: Artie: 'What are you opening with?' / Hank: '"Spinning Wheel," but with a latin flavor.' / Artie: 'Sounds like a showstopper.' / Hank: 'Oh, it is. It is.' / Artie: 'Hank, you don't open with a showstopper.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks what Hank is opening with; Hank announces 'Spinning Wheel' with a Latin flavor as his opener
jokes.punchline: Artie says 'Sounds like a showstopper' — sarcasm that Hank takes literally — then delivers the genuine showbiz wisdom/put-down: 'You don't open with a showstopper'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured two-beat joke. First Artie's sarcastic 'Sounds like a showstopper' flies over Hank's head, then the follow-up delivers both a genuine laugh AND actual showbiz advice. It works on multiple levels: Hank's obliviousness, Artie's exasperation, and the absurdity of discussing the craft of Hank's act as though it has any chance of succeeding.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You've sunk all your money in that silly restaurant, and now you're completely fucked. 100% fucked.

jokes.text: Leo's contract offer reveal — Artie says 'No offense' before showing the number, Artie says 'None taken' at the network's low offer
jokes.setup: Leo finally shows Larry and Artie the network's latest contract offer
jokes.punchline: The offer is so low that Artie pre-emptively says 'No offense' — as if the NUMBER itself is an insult he's delivering — and then Larry reacts with genuine offense
jokes.explanation: The visual joke of the unseen number lands through reaction — we never see the figure but Larry's outrage tells us everything. Solid industry-insider humor about lowball offers.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Front row center at the El Toro Civic Arena exactly 4 weeks from tonight.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I thought we were going to go after Letterman money.' Leo: 'Well, Letterman had to leave a network in order to get that kind of money. I mean, is that the kind of move you want to make?'
jokes.setup: Larry expects Letterman-level money
jokes.punchline: Leo's response is technically accurate but deeply unhelpful — he's essentially asking Larry if he wants to blow up his career to get a raise
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-insider comedy — the observation about Letterman having to blow up his NBC deal to get rich is historically accurate and bitterly funny in context. Leo's delivery of this as though it's a reasonable question is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: "Spinning Wheel," but, you know, with a Latin flavor.

jokes.text: Larry: 'It's not Leno money, is it?' / Leo: 'Oh, no, no. It's much better than that.' / Larry: 'Cause I hear he's getting fucked.' / Leo: 'Oh, he's getting fucked.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Leo are benchmarking his salary against Leno and Letterman
jokes.punchline: The frank, conspiratorial agreement that Leno 'is getting fucked' — delivered with relish by both men — is the laugh
jokes.explanation: The casual industry trash-talk about a real competitor (Leno) is vintage Larry Sanders. The repeated 'Oh, he's getting fucked' — Leo eagerly agreeing — is funny for the unsentimental showbiz worldview it reveals. Rewatch value: in hindsight, given the Tonight Show history, this line has extra resonance.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hank, you don't open with a showstopper.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Let's talk about Sanders money.' / Leo: 'What does Arsenio get?' / Artie: 'Too much.'
jokes.setup: Leo pivots to 'Sanders money' as a unique benchmark
jokes.punchline: Larry's first instinct is to benchmark against Arsenio; Artie shuts down the entire comparison with 'Too much'
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Too much' is a perfect two-word dismissal — it simultaneously comments on Arsenio's salary AND on the futility of the comparison. Pure economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I thought we were going to go after Letterman money.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.line: Well, Letterman had to leave a network in order to get that kind of money.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I want you to fight, ok?' / Leo: 'Gotcha!' — delivered with inexplicable enthusiasm
jokes.setup: Larry explains he doesn't want to fight the network himself — he wants Leo to fight
jokes.punchline: Leo's 'Gotcha!' is disproportionately enthusiastic for a man who has been visibly outmaneuvered throughout this conversation — it suggests Leo has no idea what fighting for Larry actually requires
jokes.explanation: The enthusiasm of 'Gotcha!' from a man who's clearly inadequate to the task is a nice character beat. Leo's obliviousness to his own limitations is the underlying joke.

dialogue.line: 'Cause I hear he's getting fucked.
Oh, he's getting fucked.

jokes.text: Larry's ex-wife (Francine) walks in and immediately invites Leo to dinner at Larry's house without asking Larry
jokes.setup: Larry is in the middle of contract negotiations with Leo, dreading having to fire him
jokes.punchline: Francine sweeps in and invites Leo to Larry's house for dinner, cheerfully undercutting whatever awkward distance Larry was trying to maintain
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup for the dinner scene to come. Francine's oblivious warmth creates the worst possible situation for Larry, who's about to fire Leo. The [French accent] cue for Artie inviting himself is a nice bonus beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't know. Would you just pass on that amount? All right.

jokes.text: Artie [French accent]: 'Can you feed this young hellcat, too?'
jokes.setup: Leo has just been invited to dinner; Artie sees an opportunity
jokes.punchline: Artie referring to himself as a 'young hellcat' in a French accent is pure absurdism — the contrast between the term, the accent, and Rip Torn's grizzled delivery is the joke
jokes.explanation: Only Rip Torn's Artie can casually deploy a French accent and call himself a 'young hellcat' and have it land. The joke is entirely in the gap between the words and the speaker. High character integration — this line means nothing without Artie's specific energy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Can you feed this young hellcat, too?

jokes.text: Larry (after Leo leaves): 'What? Wasn't I supposed to invite him?'
jokes.setup: Francine has just invited Leo to Larry's house for dinner while Larry is trying to phase Leo out
jokes.punchline: Larry's completely oblivious response — he genuinely doesn't understand why inviting the agent he's about to fire to dinner is a problem
jokes.explanation: Larry's social obliviousness is a running character trait. The line is efficient but not exceptional — it's doing setup work for the dinner scene cringe more than delivering a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Beverly, this is Stevie Grant.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Hi.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Beverly, my assistant. The voice on the phone.

jokes.text: Stevie to Beverly: 'Look out. She's a sassy one.' Beverly: 'I beg your pardon?'
jokes.setup: Beverly delivers a sharp line to Stevie about taking his compliment 'with a grain of salt' since he's an agent
jokes.punchline: Stevie patronizes her with 'She's a sassy one'; Beverly's icy 'I beg your pardon?' is the real punchline — the silence before Larry bails her out
jokes.explanation: Beverly's 'Well, thank you. Coming from an agent, I'll take that with a grain of salt' is itself a sharp line, and Stevie's condescending response reveals his character perfectly. The cringe of his 'sassy one' and Beverly's measured outrage is satisfying character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Coming from an agent, I'll take that with a grain of salt.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Look out. She's a sassy one.

jokes.text: Hank invites Stevie to his preview at the 'Reseda Playhouse' and puts his tickets at Will Call under 'Mr. Stevie Grant, Super-Agent, plus one'
jokes.setup: Hank is pitching his act to Stevie, hoping Stevie will represent him
jokes.punchline: The formality and grandiosity of 'Mr. Stevie Grant, Super-Agent, plus one' at will call for the Reseda Playhouse is the joke — the gap between the ceremony and the venue
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Mr. Stevie Grant, Super-Agent, plus one' is peak Hank delusion. The Reseda Playhouse as venue grounds the absurdity — it's a real place, deeply unglamorous. Good character-specific absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Look out. She's a sassy one.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I beg your pardon?

jokes.text: Stevie: 'I'm there, Hank.' — and then immediately asks what night
jokes.setup: Stevie enthusiastically commits to attending Hank's show
jokes.punchline: He immediately has to ask what night — undercutting the certainty of 'I'm there' with the practical reality that he made no actual plan
jokes.explanation: Perfect beat on Stevie's character — the agent who fires off commitments before thinking. Stevie's 'I'm there' collapses under its own weight in real time. The follow-up 'Let's play it by ear' confirms he was never going.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: She's a client. She's a big pain in the ass.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: She's very nice.

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Let's play it by ear, honcho.'
jokes.setup: Stevie said 'I'm there' then realized he doesn't know the date
jokes.punchline: 'Let's play it by ear, honcho' — the verbal equivalent of a non-commitment commitment, dressed up in fake camaraderie
jokes.explanation: The word 'honcho' is doing character work — it's the kind of empty-calorie agent-speak that coats a blow-off in warmth. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: She's a big pain in the ass. She's very nice. Well, she's an actress.

jokes.text: Larry notices Hank is wearing tap shoes and clicking around the office: 'Is it my imagination or are you clicking?'
jokes.setup: Hank has been walking around the office in tap shoes throughout the scene
jokes.punchline: Larry finally notices the clicking sound; Hank explains they're tap shoes 'for dancing, silly' — as if this is completely obvious
jokes.explanation: The visual/audio gag of Hank clicking around in tap shoes during serious conversations about contracts and agents is perfectly timed. The 'silly' from Hank — as though Larry is the unreasonable one — is the character-specific kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Your tickets will be at 'will call' under Mr. Stevie Grant, super-agent, plus one.

jokes.text: Hank asks Beverly to call Darlene about 'that 5-pound bag of sand onstage, asap'
jokes.setup: Hank has been setting up his act on the main stage
jokes.punchline: The request for a '5-pound bag of sand' — with no explanation — is pure absurdism. The specificity of the weight makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The unexplained 5-pound bag of sand request is wonderfully absurd. The 'ASAP' urgency elevates it. It demands no explanation and receives none — the confidence of the request is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Let's play it by ear, honcho.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Ok...Big guy.

jokes.text: Larry: '5-pound bag of sand?' / Artie: '5-pound bag of sand.' / Artie: 'He's doing that big tap number from Lawrence of Arabia. It's a killer.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie process the sand request
jokes.punchline: Artie explains it with complete deadpan sincerity: 'He's doing that big tap number from Lawrence of Arabia. It's a killer.' — delivered as though this is a known, respected piece of repertoire
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes. 'The big tap number from Lawrence of Arabia' is a perfectly absurd invention — there is no tap number in Lawrence of Arabia, which makes it funnier. The phrase 'It's a killer' delivered by Artie with absolute poker-face authority is the perfect Rip Torn deadpan. It demands both that the audience believe Artie is serious AND that they recognize the absurdity. The joke works on multiple levels: the non-existent source material, Artie's encyclopedic knowledge of showbiz that includes Hank's absurd act, and the confidence of 'It's a killer.' This is genuinely exceptional comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is it my imagination or are you clicking?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah. These are the, uh, tap shoes. Why? For dancing, silly.

jokes.text: Stevie closes his new deal with Larry with a handshake, then says 'I'll send some contracts over for you to sign in the morning'
jokes.setup: Larry says he likes to 'close all my deals with just a handshake'; Stevie enthusiastically agrees: 'Me too!'
jokes.punchline: Stevie immediately says he'll send contracts — undercutting the handshake agreement in the same breath
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed callback to the handshake theme. Stevie's 'Me too!' is a perfectly synchronized lie — he enthusiastically mirrors Larry's sentiment and then contradicts it in the next sentence without noticing. This is tight comedy writing. The callback to Artie's handshake complaint gives it extra resonance on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Call Darlene and tell her I need that 5-pound bag of sand onstage. ASAP.

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Just you, Larry' — re: frozen yogurt being Stevie's special gesture for his most important client
jokes.setup: Artie sarcastically asks if Stevie takes all his clients to lunch — or just buys them frozen yogurt
jokes.punchline: 'Just you, Larry' — Stevie's answer transforms the cheapness of frozen yogurt into flattery; it's a tell that his special treatment of Larry is still discount-level
jokes.explanation: Solid small joke. Frozen yogurt as the sign of special treatment is the right level of pathetic to be funny without being overdone. 'Just you, Larry' is efficient and slightly sad.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He's doing that big tap number from Lawrence of Arabia. It's a killer.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Jeez, I learned how to shake a man's hand before I learned how to wipe my own ass!'
jokes.setup: Stevie leaves without shaking Artie's hand again; Artie has complained about this before
jokes.punchline: Artie escalates his handshake philosophy to its logical extreme — developmental milestones
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most quotable line and one of the strongest jokes. The escalation from 'always supposed to shake a man's hand' to 'I learned before I could wipe my own ass' is a perfect comedic payoff on the handshake running gag. It's deeply Artie — a man whose moral code is simultaneously absurd and internally consistent. The specificity of the developmental comparison ('wipe my own ass') is what elevates it from a good line to a great one. Earns its 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Just you, Larry. Good to know.

jokes.text: Artie: 'He's got a different style, that's all.' Larry: 'That kind of style got men fragged in the corps.'
jokes.setup: Larry defends Stevie's non-handshaking style
jokes.punchline: Artie invokes military fragging — soldiers killing their own officers — as the inevitable consequence of not shaking hands
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The leap from 'bad manners in Hollywood' to 'soldiers murdered their officers for less' is pure Artie — a man who genuinely views social codes as matters of life and death. The word 'fragged' is doing enormous work: it's specific, military, darkly funny, and reveals Artie's entire worldview. This is one of Rip Torn's lines that could only come from this character.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I learned how to shake a man's hand before I learned how to wipe my own ass!

jokes.text: Artie: 'Good at what? Lunch?'
jokes.setup: Larry defends Stevie: 'It just so happens he's good.' / Artie: 'Good at what?'
jokes.punchline: 'Lunch' — Artie reducing Stevie's entire skillset to the Hollywood power-lunch
jokes.explanation: Pure economy joke. One word. Artie collapses all of Stevie's 'talent' into its actual currency: the ability to pick a good restaurant and charm over a meal. The contempt is perfectly compressed. A one-word punchline that earns every point.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Do you always fuck on the first date?

jokes.text: Larry: 'He got us Bill Murray for Friday.' Artie: 'No shit? That's right.' / Artie: [yells] 'You know all Leno's got on Friday? Sandra Bernhard and Carrot Top.'
jokes.setup: Artie questions whether Stevie is actually good at anything beyond lunch
jokes.punchline: Bill Murray versus Sandra Bernhard and Carrot Top — the contrast is the joke, and Artie's yell of excitement confirms the hierarchy
jokes.explanation: The Carrot Top name-drop as the nadir of late-night bookings is a genuine industry-insider joke. Artie's full-volume yell of triumph at the comparison is perfectly characterized. The specificity of Carrot Top (not just 'a bad comedian' but THAT comedian) makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know all Leno's got on Friday? Sandra Bernhard and Carrot Top.

jokes.text: Hank singing through the air vent: 'Talking 'bout your troubles...' — Artie's commentary: 'I told him to go with a samba, not a salsa, if he's gonna do the Latin thing'
jokes.setup: Hank's rehearsal bleeds through the air vent into the office conversation
jokes.punchline: Artie's response is not 'this is ridiculous' but a specific musical note about samba vs. salsa — he is engaged with the act on its own terms
jokes.explanation: The air-vent delivery of Hank's act is a wonderful structural device. The real joke is Artie's response: he doesn't dismiss the act, he critiques it with technical specificity. This reveals that Artie, despite his contempt, has been paying close attention — which is both funny and endearing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I told him to go with a samba, not with a salsa, if he's gonna do the Latin thing.

jokes.text: After the Stevie signing, Larry frets about Leo: 'Leo will not take this personally, huh? Right?' Artie: 'Oh, no.' Larry: 'I mean, he'll understand, won't he?' Artie: 'Of course.' Beat. 'Poor Leo.'
jokes.setup: Larry is seeking reassurance that firing his longtime agent won't destroy their friendship
jokes.punchline: Artie's hollow reassurances ('Oh, no' / 'Of course') — transparently insincere — culminate in 'Poor Leo,' which confirms everything Larry is afraid of
jokes.explanation: 'Poor Leo' as the button is excellent. The two fake reassurances set it up perfectly — we know Artie thinks this is going to be a disaster, and 'poor Leo' confirms it with maximum economy. Classic Larry Sanders pattern: false reassurance followed by honest puncture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Isn't it 'come down'?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He's scatting.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Poor Leo.'
jokes.setup: Larry worries about how Leo will take being replaced; everyone reassures him Leo won't take it personally
jokes.punchline: After Larry and Artie talk themselves into believing Leo will be fine, Artie quietly says 'Poor Leo' — a one-line deflation of their rationalization
jokes.explanation: Two words carrying the weight of an entire character observation. Artie knows exactly what's happening to Leo. The joke is in its perfect positioning — after Larry convinces himself everything will be fine, Artie's 'Poor Leo' is the pin in the balloon. Pure economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.line: Just give me my standard 10% of Larry's portion.

jokes.text: Hank (through vent): '...Must come 'round...' / Larry: 'Isn't it "come down"?' / Artie: 'He's scatting.'
jokes.setup: Hank's singing bleeds through the vent; Larry notices he's got the lyrics wrong
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat explanation — 'He's scatting' — as though this is a completely legitimate artistic choice rather than Hank not knowing the words
jokes.explanation: Artie covering for Hank's incompetence by re-framing it as artistic intent ('scatting') is a wonderful joke. The deadpan certainty of the explanation is what makes it — Artie will not concede that Hank is simply getting the lyrics wrong. High character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You wash, I'll dry.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: Larry has a dishwasher.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You rinse, I'll load.

jokes.text: The Leo dinner scene: Artie asks for ice cream, Artie: 'Dairy clogs me up, Francine. I'll stick with my salty dog.'
jokes.setup: Francine offers ice cream to the dinner guests
jokes.punchline: Artie's medical disclaimer about dairy followed by his preference for a cocktail — the salty dog — as his dessert choice
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'salty dog' as Artie's dessert alternative is good character business — he's the kind of man who always has a cocktail in hand. The medical complaint about dairy is a nice character detail.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Not the nuts.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.line: You know, Leo? Ohhh.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Goes right to my hips. I'll have a little.' — then immediately capitulates: 'I'll eat on the left side.'
jokes.setup: Larry declines ice cream citing his hips; Francine offers to give him a small amount
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately caves — 'I'll have a little' — then rationalizes it by deciding to 'eat on the left side,' as though this solves the hip problem
jokes.explanation: Larry's inability to maintain any position, even about ice cream, is a nice character note. 'I'll eat on the left side' is a perfectly Larry piece of magical thinking. Good character-specific absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No. Thick shirt.

jokes.text: Leo: 'Just give me my standard 10% of Larry's portion.'
jokes.setup: Francine serves ice cream; everyone's negotiating how much they want
jokes.punchline: Leo inserts his agent relationship into the ice cream portioning — '10% of Larry's portion' — which is simultaneously a joke about agents taking a cut of everything AND a hint of what's coming with the firing
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever joke. Leo reduces his entire professional relationship with Larry to a formula — and applies it to ice cream. It works as a self-deprecating gag AND as unconscious foreshadowing (he won't be getting his 10% much longer). The joke is both funny in the moment and gains resonance as the dinner scene unfolds.

dialogue.speaker: Doc
dialogue.line: I mean, he shit all over my career.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Right.

jokes.text: Larry confesses he had lunch with Stevie Grant; Leo reacts; Artie immediately offers to help with the dishes: 'Francine, you wash, I'll dry'
jokes.setup: Larry drops the Stevie Grant lunch bomb at the dinner table; tension rises immediately
jokes.punchline: Artie's tactical retreat to the kitchen — doing dishes — is a physical comedy of avoidance. 'Larry has a dishwasher.' 'All right, dear. You rinse, I'll load.'
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in cringe-comedy choreography. Artie sees the disaster unfolding and tries to escape via dishes, gets blocked ('Larry has a dishwasher'), then immediately pivots to loading — a man so determined to leave the room he will find any kitchen task available. The physical comedy of a Rip Torn-caliber actor doing increasingly menial kitchen work to avoid a social catastrophe is wonderful. The 'Larry has a dishwasher' correction from Francine and Artie's instant adaptation ('All right, dear. You rinse, I'll load') is beautifully timed. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Doc
dialogue.line: Just like Ed McMahon, you have an act.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, I wear many hats, you know.

dialogue.speaker: Doc
dialogue.line: Now, that's quite an act.

jokes.text: Larry's increasingly desperate attempt to manage Leo: 'I mean, if you want me to do anything differently, just tell me. I mean, is there anything that I do that annoy-- that annoys you?'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to manage the fallout of the Stevie revelation at dinner
jokes.punchline: Larry's descent into asking Leo if HE is doing anything wrong — putting the entire burden of the breakup on himself, in the most self-undermining way possible — is peak Larry Sanders insecurity
jokes.explanation: The cut-off 'annoy-- that annoys you?' is a perfect scripted stutter — Larry catching himself but unable to stop. This is Garry Shandling at his best: showing us a man who is simultaneously the agent of his own cruelty and completely unable to execute it. Strong character integration.

dialogue.line: Ok, ok, ok. Now, what's funny about that? Tell Melanie 5:30 instead of 6:00.

jokes.text: Leo: 'No. No. I just thought it was time for some changes.' / Larry: 'Well, fine.' / Leo: 'Well, fine.' / Larry: 'Well, let's-- What can we change here?' / Leo: 'Nothing.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Leo are navigating the world's most uncomfortable agent breakup at a dinner party
jokes.punchline: The Beckett-like 'Well, fine. / Well, fine. / What can we change? / Nothing.' exchange — both men trapped in politeness, each 'Well, fine' more strained than the last
jokes.explanation: This is proto-Curb, proto-Office cringe at its finest. The rhythmic exchange of 'Well, fine' volleys is structurally perfect — two men who cannot end a relationship, trapped in a loop of meaningless affirmations. The final 'Nothing' from Leo — meaning there's nothing to change, this IS the end — is devastating and funny simultaneously. The writing here is exceptional: it's four words ('Nothing') doing the work of a breakup scene. Earns its 8.

dialogue.line: He's Italian. She's from Wisconsin.
Macaroni and cheese.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'm going with Stevie. It is a business decision.' / Leo: 'Please, Leo, don't do this.' / Larry: 'Not the nuts.'
jokes.setup: Larry finally says he's going with Stevie; Leo reacts with some kind of physical gesture (reaching for nuts on the table or a physical collapse)
jokes.punchline: 'Not the nuts' — Larry's line suggests Leo is either grabbing nuts off the table, squeezing something, or making a gesture that Larry has to stop — the physical breakdown of Leo's dignity
jokes.explanation: The mystery of 'Not the nuts' — what is Leo doing with the nuts? — is the perfect cringe payoff. The visual ambiguity (are these nuts on the dinner table? Is Leo squeezing them as a stress response?) combined with Larry's horrified 'Not the nuts' is simultaneously specific and wonderfully open to interpretation. Extremely quotable out of context. The physical dignity collapse of Leo at the dinner table is the culmination of the episode's best running cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I like New York. You know, the, uh, museums, the park. You know, you can walk everywhere.

jokes.text: Doc (Billy Crystal stand-in) tells Larry: 'Leo was destroyed. You were his biggest client.' Then immediately: 'The only reason I stay with Leo is because he goes on the road with me. But he hasn't done shit for my career. He shit all over my career.'
jokes.setup: Doc expresses sympathy for Leo's devastation
jokes.punchline: Immediately pivots to complaining about Leo himself — 'he shit all over my career' — making the sympathy transparently self-serving
jokes.explanation: The lightning-speed pivot from 'Leo was destroyed' to 'he shit all over my career' is a beautiful piece of Hollywood-insider satire. Doc's sympathy lasts about four seconds before self-interest takes over. The escalation from 'hasn't done shit' to 'shit all over' is a nice linguistic gag — the vocabulary of shit doing double duty.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: I happen to, uh, you know, hate New York. But on the show, you're always talking about what a great city it is.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, um, I also happen to talk about what a great city Jacksonville is because we have affiliates there.

jokes.text: Hank: 'No, I'm trying to go easy on my pipes. Saving it for the people.'
jokes.setup: Hank approaches Doc speaking in a soft voice; Doc asks if he's okay
jokes.punchline: Hank is 'saving his voice for the people' — the grandiosity of treating his lounge act audience as 'the people' is peak Hank delusion
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank. The phrase 'saving it for the people' — as if the people are waiting — combined with the vocal protection routine is self-delusion at its most charming. Only Hank would be vocally resting before the Reseda Playhouse.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I happen to hate New York. Well, um, I also happen to talk about what a great city Jacksonville is because we have affiliates there.

jokes.text: Hank pitches his act concept to Doc: '30-piece orchestra, tuxedos, but every musician has a mustache'
jokes.setup: Hank describes the visual concept for his act
jokes.punchline: The mustache requirement — the ONLY distinguishing feature of the orchestra — as though this is the bold creative vision that makes the act
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Hank absurdism. The mustache requirement as the defining artistic statement of a 30-piece orchestra is brilliantly specific and meaningless. The logic — 'you have to have a sense of humor about yourself' — as the justification is even funnier. It's the kind of joke that works because it has an internal dream-logic: Hank has clearly thought about this deeply, which makes it more absurd, not less. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: When did this become a 'screw 'em' situation? Just roughly?

jokes.text: Doc: 'How about all bald guys?' / Hank: 'Ok, ok, ok. Now, what's funny about that?'
jokes.setup: Hank explains the mustache concept as a way of 'having a sense of humor about yourself'
jokes.punchline: Doc suggests bald musicians instead; Hank asks 'what's funny about that?' — completely missing that his own mustache concept has the same logical problem
jokes.explanation: Hank's inability to see the bald gag as equivalent to his mustache gag reveals his total lack of self-awareness. The double standard — mustaches are obviously funny, bald is not — is a perfect character note. He's critiquing someone else's logic with exactly the same logic.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Who's Francine?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah. See? Tommy, I think-- See, right there, you know?

jokes.text: Sheldon (network exec) in elevator, casually dropping: 'I was so surprised to hear that you were thinking about leaving the network.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Sheldon run into each other in the elevator going to the commissary
jokes.punchline: Sheldon reveals he knows about the Stevie/New York leverage play — Stevie has apparently been using it without Larry's knowledge — in the most casual, elevator-small-talk register possible
jokes.explanation: The elevator as the setting for this bombshell is perfect — Larry is trapped, nowhere to go, doors haven't opened yet. The casualness of Sheldon's delivery ('I was so surprised...') masks what is essentially an ambush. Good structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Could be worse. You could be in Leno's band.

jokes.text: Sheldon: 'This is your way of firing me, Sheldon?' — Larry's paranoid misread of the situation
jokes.setup: Sheldon says he heard Larry wants to leave the network
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant defensive counter-attack: 'Is this your way of firing me?' — his anxiety turns the situation on its head before he even has information
jokes.explanation: Larry's paranoia perfectly expressed: the person who's allegedly about to quit immediately assumes he's being fired. Classic Larry Sanders character comedy — his insecurity always attacks before it defends.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I think I'm just gonna sing the 'bwaa.' I mean, you know, make it like a joke. That's funny, huh?

jokes.text: Sheldon casually mentions Larry 'moving to New York' as established fact; Larry has no idea this is part of the plan
jokes.setup: Larry didn't know Stevie was using New York as a leverage play
jokes.punchline: Larry's flailing: 'Well, new york? I have mixed emotions about that, you know?' — desperately playing along with information he doesn't have
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'mixed emotions' about a move he didn't know he was making is a good cringe-comedy beat. The improvisational quality of his cover — 'I like New York. You know, the museums, the park, you can walk everywhere' — sounds exactly like a man buying time.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hank has got a pair of cojones the size of Texas. You gotta give him that.

jokes.text: Larry: '...the, uh, Museums, the park. You know, you can walk everywhere.' — selling New York he's never agreed to move to
jokes.setup: Larry has to spontaneously sell the idea that he WANTS to move to New York
jokes.punchline: His list of New York's merits — 'museums, the park, you can walk everywhere' — is the most tepid possible endorsement of New York City from a man who clearly has no intention of moving there
jokes.explanation: The specific vagueness of his New York endorsement is funny — he's reached into the most generic bag of 'things people like about New York' and come up with nothing that suggests genuine desire to move.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Do any of you guys have a bassoon in your car or-- A bassoon? Yeah.

jokes.text: Sheldon: 'Well, of course, it isn't his career he's playing with.'
jokes.setup: Sheldon and Larry agree that Stevie grant has 'no fears' as a tough negotiator
jokes.punchline: Sheldon's perfectly timed observation: Stevie can be fearless because it's Larry's career on the line, not his own
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry observation perfectly delivered. The economy is exceptional — this one sentence captures everything wrong with the agent-client power dynamic. Sheldon saying it with bemused sympathy rather than alarm makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: It's the worst piece of shit I've ever seen. Hey, you should really consider replacing him if New York happens.

jokes.text: Sheldon: 'I wish you happiness wherever you land, lar. And I mean that from my heart as a friend.' — Larry's reaction: 'What a pain in the ass.'
jokes.setup: Sheldon wraps up the elevator conversation with elaborate sincerity
jokes.punchline: The moment the doors close (or Sheldon exits), Larry mutters 'What a pain in the ass' — the standard Hollywood warmth revealed as performance
jokes.explanation: The 'from my heart as a friend' sincerity immediately followed by Larry's 'what a pain in the ass' is a classic Larry Sanders beat. It punctures the Hollywood warmth theatrics efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: How can you stand it? It's the worst piece of shit I've ever seen.

jokes.text: Stevie explains the New York play; Larry: 'I happen to, uh, you know, hate New York.' / Stevie: 'But on the show you're always talking about what a great city it is.' / Larry: 'Well, I also happen to talk about what a great city Jacksonville is because we have affiliates there.'
jokes.setup: Stevie catches Larry saying he hates New York after Larry told Sheldon he loves it
jokes.punchline: Larry's explanation: everything he says on the show is affiliate management, not personal opinion — Jacksonville is great BECAUSE affiliates. This perfectly captures the hollow geography of late-night TV.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a piece of genuine industry satire. The Jacksonville line is a perfect piece of showbiz cynicism — it explains the entire geography of late-night enthusiasm with one sentence. The implication that Larry has NEVER meant anything he's said about American cities on his show is both funny and plausible. High originality, economy, and character integration: only a late-night host character in a showbiz satire can deliver this revelation. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: You're a quadruple threat. You're a singer, a dancer, a raconteur, and a singer again because you're just that good.

jokes.text: Stevie: 'If we can't make a deal with one of the networks, screw 'em!' / Larry: 'When did this become a "screw 'em" situation? Just roughly?'
jokes.setup: Stevie enthusiastically introduces syndication as a possibility without warning
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Just roughly?' — the perfectly understated addition to his genuine alarm
jokes.explanation: 'When did this become a screw 'em situation? Just roughly?' is vintage Larry Sanders voice. The 'Just roughly?' addition is what elevates this from a good complaint to a great one — the sardonic qualification, as though he'd accept a very rough timeline for when his career became an all-or-nothing gamble.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's 2-faced, and he's weird. He's just plain weird, Artie.

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Just remember one thing. If anybody asks, you're dying to move to New York.' Larry: 'You know, that is easy for you to say.'
jokes.setup: Stevie wraps up his pitch with a directive
jokes.punchline: Larry's deflated 'That is easy for you to say' — a perfectly defeated line that acknowledges Stevie is gambling with Larry's home, not his own
jokes.explanation: A callback beat to Sheldon's observation. The line itself is simple but the delivery and context make it land. Larry is genuinely put-upon and the audience feels it.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Hank fired his agent this afternoon. Because he thinks that Stevie's gonna represent him, right?

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Trust nobody on this! Hey, trust nobody on this, Larry. Promise me.' Larry (whispering): 'Oh, man.' Stevie: 'Can I just tell Francine?' Larry: 'I'd rather you didn't.' Stevie: '[mutters]'
jokes.setup: Stevie instructs Larry to keep the New York leverage secret from everyone
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately asks if he can tell Francine — his first instinct being to break the rule just established — and then Stevie refuses, which makes Larry mutter darkly
jokes.explanation: Larry's instinct to immediately violate the trust he just agreed to is very Larry. The reversal of speaker — Larry asking Stevie for permission to tell his own wife — is a funny power-dynamic joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Little prick. Sickening.

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Who's Francine?' — having no idea who Larry's wife is
jokes.setup: Larry asks to tell 'Francine' the secret; Stevie has been acting as his intimate confidant and partner
jokes.punchline: Stevie doesn't know who Francine is — he's Larry's agent and closest business confidant, but doesn't know his wife's name. Reveals how surface-level his 'intimacy' is
jokes.explanation: Three words that demolish Stevie's entire pose as Larry's closest ally. 'Who's Francine?' exposes the shallowness of all his bonding with perfect economy. It also lands as a commentary on the whole agent-client relationship — the agent knows your leverage but not your life. One of the episode's best structural comedy beats.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: See you Friday, Stevie!

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Trust nobody on this!' — then immediately asks 'Who's Francine?'
jokes.setup: Stevie instructs Larry to 'trust nobody' with the New York gambit
jokes.punchline: Stevie himself doesn't know who Francine is — a fundamental fact about Larry's life — exposing how little Stevie actually knows about his client
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed joke. Stevie tells Larry to 'trust nobody' — positioning himself as the insider who knows everything — and then immediately reveals he doesn't know who Francine is. Larry's reaction ('Yeah. See? Right there.') confirms the irony. This is tight, well-calibrated comedy writing: the joke is entirely structural, requiring no exaggeration or mugging to land. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Hank tells the bandleader he needs a bassoon in the chorus — 'Do any of you guys have a bassoon in your car?'
jokes.setup: Hank is demanding increasingly specific musical additions to his 'Spinning Wheel' arrangement
jokes.punchline: The specificity of the bassoon request — and the completely sincere follow-up asking if anyone brought one in their car — is perfectly absurdist
jokes.explanation: The bassoon-in-the-car request is a great escalation of Hank's increasingly impossible demands. Bassoons are particularly funny woodwind instruments to invoke — they're obscure, expensive, and comically unwieldy. 'In your car' grounds the absurdity in logistics.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You could be in Leno's band.' (to the musical director complaining about Hank's rehearsal)
jokes.setup: The bandleader expresses frustration at having to participate in Hank's act
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Could be worse. You could be in Leno's band.' — Leno's band as the nadir of late-night musical employment
jokes.explanation: The Leno-as-consolation-prize joke is perfectly economical. Artie weaponizes the Leno rivalry in Hank's defense, and it works as both industry satire and a genuine put-down of the Tonight Show's cultural status.

jokes.text: Hank asks how much the horns would cost — is told the figure — then decides he'll just 'sing the bwaa.' 'Make it like a joke. That's funny, huh?'
jokes.setup: Hank wants horns for the 'bwaa' moment in 'Spinning Wheel'; the cost is prohibitive
jokes.punchline: Hank's solution: he'll vocally imitate the horn sound himself and call it intentional comedy. 'That's funny, huh?' — seeking validation for his compromise
jokes.explanation: Hank's ability to reframe every limitation as an artistic choice is his defining character trait. The 'bwaa' becoming a 'joke' because he can't afford horns is beautifully pathetic. 'That's funny, huh?' seeking endorsement from his band is the vulnerability underneath the delusion.

jokes.text: Hank's full 'Spinning Wheel' performance with the 'bwaa' ending and a visible stumble: '♪ Got no money-- uhh! ♪'
jokes.setup: Hank performs his act for Artie and the band; we've been building to this all episode
jokes.punchline: The performance includes an audible stumble/injury mid-lyric ('uhh!') — Hank injures himself during his showstopper, the physical comedy payoff of the entire act subplot
jokes.explanation: The entire Hank act subplot pays off here. The 'uhh!' mid-performance is the perfect understated physical comedy — it doesn't stop the show, it just emerges in the lyric like a natural event. Rewatch bonus because you can see it coming once you know the episode.

jokes.text: Hank performs the full 'Spinning Wheel' on the stage — live — including the 'bwaaa' and a stumble: '♪ Got no money— uhh! ♪'
jokes.setup: After all the rehearsal discussion, Hank performs the number for Artie and the band
jokes.punchline: The performance itself — visible stumble mid-lyric ('uhh!'), the earnest delivery, the 'bwaa' replacement — is the comedic payoff to the entire Hank subplot
jokes.explanation: The performance is the payoff to the entire Hank subplot and earns its place. Jeffrey Tambor's earnest commitment to the terrible performance would be where most of the laughs live. The 'uhh!' stumble written into the lyrics is a perfect visual gag made audible.

jokes.text: Artie watching Hank perform — 'Hank has got a pair of cojones the size of Texas. You gotta give him that.'
jokes.setup: Artie is watching Hank rehearse the full act.
jokes.punchline: 'Cojones the size of Texas' — Artie's grudging respect for Hank's sheer audacity is a character reversal that works as both comedy and genuine warmth. It's the Artie-Hank relationship in one line.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most memorable lines. The grudging, specific admiration ('cojones the size of Texas') from Artie — who has been demolishing Hank all episode — is a perfect character beat. It's funny AND it deepens the Artie/Hank relationship. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Artie watching the performance: 'Hank has got a pair of cojones the size of Texas. You gotta give him that.'
jokes.setup: Hank's performance is objectively terrible; Artie and Stevie watch from the side
jokes.punchline: Artie's grudging respect — not for the quality of the act, but for the sheer audacity of attempting it — is the funniest possible response
jokes.explanation: Artie's backhanded tribute is pure character comedy. The 'cojones the size of Texas' line is Artie finding the one genuinely positive thing he can say about Hank's act: it's not talent, it's nerve. The visual of Artie watching this disaster with solemn appreciation is gold.

jokes.text: Stevie to Larry: 'Hank just forced me to sit through that act of his. How can you stand it? What, that bad, was it? It's the worst piece of shit I've ever seen.'
jokes.setup: Stevie has just told Hank his act was 'excellent'
jokes.punchline: The instant the Hank-Stevie interaction ends, Stevie tells Larry it's 'the worst piece of shit I've ever seen'
jokes.explanation: The structural irony of this is perfect — Stevie's two-faced nature (which has been building all episode) is encapsulated in the gap between 'excellent' and 'worst piece of shit I've ever seen.' Good callback to his character arc.

jokes.text: Stevie to Hank (face): 'It was excellent, Hank. It was just excellent.' / 'You're a quadruple threat. You're a singer, a dancer, a raconteur, and a singer again, because you're just that good.'
jokes.setup: Hank appears and Stevie immediately performs rapturous approval
jokes.punchline: 'A singer, a dancer, a raconteur, and a singer again' — the 'and a singer again' because Stevie can't think of a fourth quality is both an insult and a backhanded compliment
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's second-best joke. The 'quadruple threat' structure is the key: 'singer, dancer, raconteur...' promises a fourth distinct talent, but Stevie loops back to 'singer again' with 'because you're just that good' as cover. It's a masterclass in fake flattery — Stevie can't even invent a fourth virtue, so he repeats one and makes it sound like abundance. The irony layer (we just heard 'worst piece of shit') makes it devastating. High quotability.

jokes.text: Stevie tells Hank his act was 'excellent' and calls him 'a quadruple threat: singer, dancer, raconteur, and a singer again — because you're just that good'
jokes.setup: Hank catches Stevie watching; Stevie needs to say something
jokes.punchline: 'A quadruple threat: singer, dancer, raconteur, and a singer again' — the 'singer again' undermining the entire construct while sounding like a compliment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Quadruple threat' sets up a triumphant list; 'singer, dancer, raconteur' sounds impressive; 'and a singer again — because you're just that good' is the perfect collapse. The repetition of 'singer' as the fourth element is the formal joke — Stevie couldn't think of a fourth talent — but framing the repetition as proof of exceptional ability ('just that good') is the character joke. Highly quotable, beautifully structured, pure Stevie. Rewatch bonus: you can see him desperately improvising.

jokes.text: Hank fires his agent because he thinks Stevie will represent him; Artie: 'Uh-oh. What, you stick yourself?'
jokes.setup: Larry learns Hank has fired his agent based on Stevie's encouragement; the audience already knows Stevie called the act 'the worst piece of shit I've ever seen'
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Uh-oh' followed by the non-sequitur 'What, you stick yourself?' — presumably reacting to Larry with a pin or craft item, the joke being the collision of this small physical slapstick with the larger disaster
jokes.explanation: The 'stick yourself' line is a small physical comedy beat that grounds the larger disaster. The collision of scale — Artie notices Larry's minor injury while processing Hank's career catastrophe — is good situational comedy.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I hate that little prick. He's a liar. It's sickening, Artie. I don't care if this is the way people do business in show business.'
jokes.setup: Larry processes Stevie's treatment of Hank
jokes.punchline: The irony is that Larry DOES participate in showbiz ethics constantly — the entire episode is him navigating the same two-faced system. His moral outrage is entirely selective.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the irony of Larry's moral outrage — he just did basically the same thing to Leo. Not the show's sharpest joke but solid character irony.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Leo's not right either. I don't know what to do. I can't stay with Stevie — he's two-faced and he's weird. He's just plain weird, Artie.'
jokes.setup: Artie suggests going back to Leo; Larry rejects this too
jokes.punchline: 'He's just plain weird' — after 'two-faced' and dishonest, the final charge against Stevie is that he's 'weird.' The specificity of 'just plain weird' as a dealbreaker next to ethical violations is classic Larry
jokes.explanation: The escalation from serious charges (dishonesty) to 'just plain weird' is a great Larry comedy beat. His ultimate deal-breaker is aesthetic/social discomfort rather than ethics. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Stevie drops a new contract offer, then Larry fires him in the most anticlimactic possible way: 'Yeah, yeah. Ok, then. Good, thanks. Ok, then.'
jokes.setup: Larry sets up an elaborate speech about firing Stevie — 'there are a lot of things on my mind that I want to mention to you'
jokes.punchline: After the big buildup, the firing is dispensed with in three 'ok, thens' — the most passive, inarticulate dismissal possible
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Larry builds up to the firing with the weight of 'I have a lot of things I want to mention to you' — suggesting a thorough accounting of Stevie's crimes — and then executes it in three filler phrases. 'Yeah, yeah. Ok, then. Good, thanks. Ok, then.' This is peak Garry Shandling — the man who can't confront anything directly doing the most minimal possible version of a firing. The structure (big setup, nothing punchline) is the entire joke. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Larry starts a big speech to Stevie: 'I've been thinking today about a lot of stuff and I have a lot of things on my mind that I want to mention to you...' [Stevie hands him an improved contract offer]
jokes.setup: Larry has spent the scene building up to firing Stevie; he begins an elaborate windup
jokes.punchline: Stevie cuts it off by handing Larry a contract — the implicit suggestion being the offer is so good Larry might fold — and we cut away before we hear what Larry does
jokes.explanation: The structural misdirection here is well done — we expect the firing speech, Stevie counters with the one thing that could derail it. The comedy is in the interruption of Larry's elaborate buildup.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Little prick. Sickening.' / Larry and Artie share a beat of silence / Larry: 'Oh, Larry, are we going to the Dodgers game tomorrow night, or is that Friday?' / Artie: 'Friday.'
jokes.setup: Stevie has just been fired; Larry and Artie are left in the aftermath
jokes.punchline: The immediate pivot to the Dodgers game — scheduling a recreational outing like nothing happened — is the perfect deflation of the entire episode's emotional and professional upheaval
jokes.explanation: The Larry Sanders Show's signature move: the catastrophic event absorbed instantly into the mundane. After all the agent drama, Leo heartbreak, and Hank's career crisis, the episode ends on 'Are we going to the Dodgers game?' The simplicity and totality of the pivot is the joke. 'Friday.' is the perfect Artie period. This is what proto-Curb felt like before Larry David formalized it.

jokes.text: Larry (calling out as Stevie leaves): 'See you Friday, Stevie!'
jokes.setup: Larry has just fired Stevie in the most passive way imaginable; Artie and Larry have moved on to Dodgers game planning
jokes.punchline: Larry cheerfully calls 'See you Friday, Stevie!' as Stevie departs — either genuinely forgetting he just fired him, or doing it to be cruel, both equally funny and character-specific
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and one of its best. 'See you Friday, Stevie!' is delivered with complete Larry Sanders ambiguity — is he inviting the man he just fired to the Dodgers game? Has he already forgotten? Is this cruelty? The genius is that all three readings are simultaneously true and funny. It recontextualizes the Dodgers game exchange as potentially including Stevie. The closer has the confidence of a show that trusts its own voice completely.

tmdb_overview: Larry decides he needs a new high-power agent to negotiate his new deal with the network.
